items.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: I remember him telling me... listening to the way Lester Young starts the band off... Buck Clayton and Harry 'Sweets' Edison on trumpets

ctx.x: I want to talk about another aspect here. Of course we’re doing our archive here principally based upon the life of Joe Williams and the chronology of the Count Basie band. And I’d like for you to just give us some insights into how the Kansas City scene that spawned some of the great midwestern territory bands and eventually of course the great Count Basie band, how that would have been different from what was happening on either coast, and some of its distinctives.

Well I think it had a lot of the same ingredients that were in the other regional jazzes, if we can say that, but I think their blues were a little different kind of blues and I think eventually they ended up calling it “urban blues” as opposed to “country blues.” But it was the rhythm. The way they smoothed out the rhythm. They got that four-four like it was on ball bearings or big rubber tires or something, but it flowed in a way that no other jazz flowed, and I think it had an infectious feeling to it. And all…

and probably his favorite band was the Basie band. So that was what I cut my teeth on, among other bands. And I remember him telling me, “Listen to the way Lester Young starts the band off on ‘Every Tub.’” Because he had the first lick before the band even came in. And my brother was twelve years older than I was and you know, he was like a second father in a way. He used to take me out with his friends and, you know, I looked up to him and I found that this interest he had touched me. I didn’t have to think…
